raw_findings.message: The built-in operator token is present in the source and used as the default authorization secret, allowing anyone who knows it to run privileged commands.
Floating-point interest calculation loses cent precision for sufficiently large balances, so interest credited can differ from exact integer arithmetic.
When spending exceeds the limit, wrapping subtraction turns the remaining allowance into a huge value and permits further transfers.
An empty recipient list makes the divisor zero, so `split` panics when invoked without recipients.
An out-of-range account index panics instead of returning an error, and a user can trigger this through `account-at`.
Opening an already-used account name creates duplicate records while lookups and mutations select only the first, making subsequent operations ambiguous and potentially inaccessible.
Balance mutations use unchecked signed arithmetic, so sufficiently large deposits or other balance operations can overflow and corrupt balances in release builds.
A negative transfer passes the funds check and is queued, causing settlement to credit the source and debit the destination.
A transfer rejected for exceeding the daily allowance resets all prior spending, allowing a later transfer to bypass the limit.
Settlement credits destinations without checking whether they are closed, so a transfer queued before closure can change a closed account's balance.
Fees are applied without checking the daily limit, so a positive fee can push spending beyond the configured limit.
A negative fee increases the account balance, and its cast to `u64` on the next line also wraps the daily-spend counter.
Every operation appends an audit entry indefinitely and persistence retains all entries, so repeated commands can exhaust memory or disk.
Non-numeric monetary arguments panic because parsing unwraps the error, allowing malformed CLI or batch input to terminate the process.
Joining an unvalidated output name permits `..` components or an absolute path, allowing statements to be written outside the reports directory.
A negative daily limit is cast from `i64` to `u64`, becoming an enormous limit that effectively disables spending restrictions.
Account names are serialized without escaping delimiters or newlines, so a crafted name can inject additional records into the persisted ledger.

fixed_raw_findings.message: The spend counter is only incremented and never reset by day, so after an account uses its daily allowance it remains unable to transfer that amount on subsequent days.
Settlement subtracts queued amounts without checking the source's current balance, so a fee or adjustment made after queuing can cause a transfer to overdraw the account.
Adding a transfer to the destination balance is unchecked, so settling into an account near `i64::MAX` wraps in release builds and corrupts its balance.
A fee is subtracted without checking available funds, so `fee acct <amount>` can make an account balance negative.
The validated report path can still name a symlink inside `reports/`, so writing a statement can overwrite the symlink's target outside that directory.
Malformed persisted numeric fields are silently replaced with zero, so a corrupted state file can erase balances or limits when the next command saves it.
Account names are written into the line-oriented state format without escaping, so a name containing a newline and crafted record can inject accounts or other state records on the next load.

raw_findings.message: The operator token is embedded in the source and is used as the default credential, so anyone who knows the code can authorize `close` and `adjust` when no environment token is configured.
Interest is calculated through `f64`, which cannot represent all large cent balances exactly, so valid balances can be credited a cent amount different from integer arithmetic.
When spending exceeds the limit, `wrapping_sub` turns the remaining allowance into a huge value, allowing subsequent transfers to bypass the daily limit.
An empty recipient list makes `split_payment` divide by zero, so invoking `split` with only an amount panics.
`account_at` indexes without validating the index, so an out-of-range or negative CLI index panics and terminates the process.
Opening an existing account name creates another account with the same name, making lookups and balance-changing operations ambiguous and potentially leaving duplicate balances in the ledger.
A negative deposit is accepted as an unvalidated withdrawal, letting callers reduce an account balance without checking funds or charging daily spending.

Balance mutations use unchecked signed arithmetic, so sufficiently large deposits, transfers, fees, interest, or adjustments can overflow and corrupt balances in release builds or panic in debug builds.
Negative transfer amounts pass the balance check and are settled with reversed signs, allowing a queued transfer to move money from the named recipient to the source.
Each queued transfer is checked only against the current balance and not other pending debits, so multiple individually accepted transfers can settle to a negative source balance.
Rejecting an over-limit transfer resets the source account's spent counter, and the caller persists this mutation even on error, so repeated rejected requests can bypass the daily limit.
Settlement does not check whether an account is closed, so a transfer queued before closure can still credit the closed destination.
A negative fee is accepted, credits the account, and is cast to `u64` when updating spending, wrapping the counter to a huge value.
Fees increase the spending counter without checking the daily limit, so an arbitrarily large fee can exceed the configured limit.
Every operation appends an audit entry without any bound or pruning, so repeated commands grow the state file and memory use indefinitely.
Numeric command arguments are parsed with `unwrap`, so a non-numeric amount or limit panics and terminates the CLI instead of returning an input error.
Statements include the ledger-wide audit log rather than entries for the requested account, so anyone able to request a statement can see other accounts' activity and transaction amounts.
The user-supplied report name is joined without restricting traversal or absolute paths, so `statement --out` can overwrite files outside the reports directory.
A negative daily limit parses as `i64` and is cast to `u64`, turning it into an enormous limit that effectively disables transfer limits.
Invalid persisted balances are silently replaced with zero, so a malformed or truncated state file can silently erase account funds rather than failing safely.
Account names are written into the line-oriented state format without escaping, so a name containing newlines and crafted record text can inject ledger records when the state is loaded again.
State is overwritten directly with no locking or atomic update, so concurrent CLI invocations can load the same old ledger and overwrite one another's successful changes.

Settlement adds a transfer amount to the destination balance without checked arithmetic, so queuing a transfer and then adjusting the destination near `i64::MAX` can panic or wrap its balance.

A statement includes the ledger-wide recent audit log rather than entries for the requested account, so anyone able to request one account's statement can see activity and account names belonging to other accounts.
`fs::write` follows symlinks in `reports`, so a pre-created `reports/<name>` symlink can make a statement overwrite a file outside the reports directory despite the filename check.
The operator token is accepted as a command-line argument, exposing it in process argument listings to other local users while the command runs.
A malformed persisted balance is silently replaced with zero, and subsequent commands can save that altered ledger over the original state instead of rejecting the corrupt file.

Account names are written into the line-oriented state file without escaping delimiters or newlines, so an account name containing `|` and a newline can inject records that are loaded as other accounts or pending transfers.

raw_findings.message: When `BANK_OPERATOR_TOKEN` is unset, the built-in token authorizes `close` and `adjust`, so anyone who knows this source-embedded value can perform operator actions.
Interest is calculated with `f64` and truncated to cents, so sufficiently large balances can receive an incorrect amount due to floating-point precision loss.
If spending exceeds the limit, `wrapping_sub` reports a huge allowance instead of zero, allowing later transfers to bypass the daily limit.
Calling `split` without recipients divides by zero and panics the process.
An index outside the account vector, including a negative CLI index cast to `usize`, panics instead of returning an error.
Opening an already-used name appends a second account, while name lookups continue selecting the first, making the new account inaccessible through normal name-based operations.
Balance arithmetic is unchecked, so a deposit that pushes an account beyond `i64` range panics in debug builds or wraps the balance in release builds.
A negative deposit is accepted as a withdrawal without transfer-limit checks, allowing callers to remove funds through the deposit command.
Negative transfer amounts pass the balance check and are queued, so settlement credits the source and debits the destination.
Queued transfers are checked against the unchanged current balance rather than reserving funds, so multiple individually valid transfers can settle to a negative source balance.
Rejecting an over-limit transfer resets all prior spending to zero, allowing a caller to retry and then spend beyond the daily limit.
Successful spending only increments `spent_today_cents` and no code resets it at a day boundary, so the nominal daily limit persists across days unless an over-limit request resets it.
Settlement credits queued transfers without checking whether the destination was closed, so a transfer queued before closure still changes the closed account's balance.
A negative fee increases the account balance and casts the negative amount to `u64`, wrapping the spending counter to a huge value.
Every operation appends an audit entry indefinitely, so repeated commands can grow the persisted state and in-memory ledger without limit.
A non-numeric amount reaches `unwrap()` and panics the process instead of producing a handled input error.
A statement includes the ledger-wide audit log rather than entries for the requested account, exposing other accounts' activity in that statement.
The supplied statement filename is joined without restricting traversal or absolute paths, allowing `statement --out` to write outside the reports directory.
A negative daily limit is cast from `i64` to `u64`, turning it into a very large limit that can effectively disable transfer limits.
Account names are serialized without escaping `|` or newlines, so a crafted name can inject or corrupt line-oriented state records when the ledger is saved.
State is overwritten without locking or transactional updates, so concurrent CLI invocations can load the same old ledger and silently overwrite one another's changes.

lost-update-race in `save` (line 67, CWE-362): State is overwritten without locking or transactional updates, so concurrent CLI invocations can load the same old ledger and silently overwrite one another's changes.

fixed_raw_findings.message: Settlement does not recheck the source balance after a transfer is queued, so a subsequent fee or adjustment can reduce the balance and settlement can overdraw the account.
Adding a settled transfer to the recipient uses unchecked arithmetic, so crediting an account near `i64::MAX` can panic in debug builds or wrap its balance in release builds.
A fee is subtracted without checking available funds, so `fee a 200` can turn an account with 100 cents into a negative balance.
A statement includes the ledger-wide recent audit entries rather than entries for the requested account, exposing other accounts' activity to anyone who requests a statement.
Malformed persisted balances are silently converted to zero, so loading a corrupted or tampered state file can silently erase an account's balance instead of rejecting the state.
Account names are serialized without escaping delimiters or newlines, so an account name containing crafted record text can inject records into the state file when it is saved.
